solution:
The chapter lists the availability of water first among the things that decide where settlements form in India, along with climatic factors, the slope of the land and the level of development.

Water is needed every day and cannot be carried far, so people settle where there is a dependable supply of it — for drinking, for their animals and above all for growing food. That is why nucleated settlements are found in the plateau region of the Narmada Valley, in the paddy lands of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh and in other cultivated parts of the country.

The same rule works in Brazil. The chapter says the eastern coastal region is densely settled although its climate is hot and humid and its flat land limited, because it has a good water supply and a large range of natural resources.

The earliest settlements in Brazil were formed by settlers from Europe, mainly in the coastal areas, and those settlements have since developed and become densely populated.

The chapter gives the reasons. Although the coastal climate is hot and humid and flat land is limited because of the rugged topography, the region has a good water supply and a large range of natural resources. Sao Paulo is its example: it has an extensive area of rich soil ideal for growing coffee, a large supply of natural minerals close by such as iron ore, a steady energy supply, and the south-eastern area has a good transport system as well. All of this together makes the Sao Paulo area a nucleated settlement.

The interior offers none of that. Settlements become sparse towards the central part of Brazil because the area is covered by thick dense equatorial rainforest, the climate there is unhealthy and unfit for settlement, there are limitations on the use and exploitation of natural resources, and transport links in the region are poor.

The urban population of India is increasing, and the chapter names the reasons: the expansion of existing urban centres and the emergence of new towns have both played a significant role in the growth of the urban population and of urbanisation in the country. India also has a long tradition of urban life to build on — Indraprastha (Delhi), Mithila, Varanasi, Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Ujjain and Pratishthan (Paithan) were urban settlements of earlier times.

The growth has been strongest where the conditions favour it. Urbanisation has been more in the southern part of India than in the northern part; Delhi is more than 80 per cent urban, Goa is the most urbanised State with 62 per cent of its population in urban areas, and Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Kerala are also more urbanised.

[Note: the chapter itself does NOT describe India's urbanisation as rapid. It says plainly that the growth of urbanisation in India has been slow, and that the level in 2011 was 31.16 per cent, which is quite low in comparison with developed countries. What is true is that the urban population is increasing; the pace the question assumes is not what the chapter states.]

The chapter says that rural areas such as the north-east Highlands of Brazil suffer from extreme droughts.

Where the droughts are extreme it is difficult to practise agriculture, and where farming cannot be relied on, people cannot settle in numbers. So settlements there are sparse and scattered rather than gathered into villages.

The contrast with the eastern coastal strip makes the point: there a good water supply and a large range of natural resources let dense, nucleated settlements grow.

The level of urbanisation is measured as the percentage of urban population to total population, and by that measure most of India is still not highly urbanised: the level in 2011 was 31.16 per cent, which the chapter calls quite low in comparison with developed countries, and it says the growth of urbanisation in India has been slow.

The chapter's table of urban population by State shows the same thing. Only Chandigarh and the NCT of Delhi fall in the highest category, 81 to 100 per cent. Goa, Puducherry, Daman and Diu and Lakshadweep are in the 61 to 80 band; Gujarat, Maharashtra, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Mizoram in the 41 to 60 band; a long list of States in the 21 to 40 band; and Himachal Pradesh, Bihar, Assam and Odisha in the lowest band of all, 0 to 20 per cent.

So apart from the two small, almost wholly urban units of Delhi and Chandigarh, every other part of India has a much lower level of urbanisation.

[Note: Delhi and Chandigarh are city territories with very little rural area, which is why they stand apart from the States.]

**Level.** Brazil is one of the few developing countries which is highly urbanised: about 86 per cent of its population lives in urban areas. India's level in 2011 was 31.16 per cent, which the chapter calls quite low in comparison with developed countries. So Brazil is far more urbanised than India.

**Pace.** The chapter says the growth of urbanisation in India has been slow, while Brazil's substantial urban growth process is unique and is one of the underlying factors contributing to its present-day rapid economic growth.

**Where it has happened.** In Brazil rapid urbanisation happened mainly in the South and South-east, with Sao Paulo emerging as a major metropolitan and industrial area; figure 7.6 shows urbanisation to be greater in the coastal states than in the interior, with Sao Paulo, Goias and Minas Gerais more urban than the states of the North. In India urbanisation has been more in the southern part than in the northern part — Goa is the most urbanised State at 62 per cent and Delhi is more than 80 per cent urban, with Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Kerala also more urbanised, while Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Bihar and Rajasthan have low levels.

**Policy.** Because Brazil's growth is concentrated in a few parts of the country, its government is promoting a 'Go West' policy, which will reduce the pressure on those areas and reduce regional imbalance.

**A caution the chapter itself gives:** the definition of 'urban' is not very clear in Brazil, so the two percentages are not measured in exactly the same way.

**Ganga river basin.** This is one of the most closely settled parts of India. Its settlements are nucleated — the chapter names the paddy lands of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh among the regions where nucleated settlements are found — because the land is flat and cultivable, water is plentiful and agriculture has supported people there for centuries. Villages are large and close together, and the basin also carries old and important urban settlements; the chapter names Indraprastha (Delhi), Mithila and Varanasi among the urban settlements of earlier times.

**Amazon river basin.** This is one of the most thinly settled parts of Brazil. Settlements there are sparse and dispersed, and occur only in a few places. The chapter gives the reasons: the area is covered by thick dense equatorial rainforest, the climate is unhealthy and unfit for settlement, there are limitations on the use and exploitation of natural resources, and transport links are poor. Because the population is less in the Amazon basin, urbanisation there is also less, though Manaus, a port at the confluence of the Negro and the Amazon, has grown.

So the two basins are opposites: a flat, fertile, well-watered plain that has carried dense nucleated settlement for centuries, against a forested, flooded, hard-to-reach lowland where settlement is scattered and rare.

Settlements grow where the conditions of life are favourable, and those conditions are not spread evenly over the earth.

The chapter names what decides it in India: climatic factors, the availability of water, the slope of the land and the level of development. Nucleated settlements are therefore found in the plateau region of the Narmada Valley, the paddy lands of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, the Vindhyan Plateau and other cultivated parts — all places with level, cultivable land and dependable water. Dispersed settlements are found in the tribal parts of central India, eastern and southern Rajasthan, the Himalayan slopes and land with dissected and uneven topography, where those conditions are missing.

The same holds for Brazil. The eastern coastal region drew settlers and grew dense because it has a good water supply and a large range of natural resources; Sao Paulo grew into a nucleated settlement because it has rich soil for coffee, minerals such as iron ore close by, a steady energy supply and a good transport system. The interior stayed empty because it is covered by thick dense equatorial rainforest, its climate is unhealthy and unfit for settlement, its resources are hard to use and its transport links are poor, and the north-east Highlands stayed empty because extreme droughts make agriculture difficult.

So people gather where there is water, workable land, resources and a way of reaching the place, and stay away from mountains, deserts, dense forests and land that cannot be farmed.
